what_its_for: Moxifloxacin is an antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, including lung infections like pneumonia, sinus infections, skin infections, and eye infections (eye drop form). It works by killing the bacteria that are causing your infection. It will NOT work for viral infections like the common cold or flu.
how_to_take: Take the tablet by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time each day so you do not forget. If you are using the eye drops (Vigamox), wash your hands first, tilt your head back, pull down your lower eyelid, and place the drop in the pocket formed. Close your eye gently for 1 to 2 minutes. Do not touch the dropper tip to your eye or any surface. Finish all of your medication even if you feel better, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: The usual adult dose for the tablet is 400 mg taken once a day. Treatment usually lasts 5 to 21 days depending on your type of infection. For eye drops, the typical dose is 1 drop in the affected eye 3 times a day for 7 days. Always follow the exact dose and schedule your doctor prescribed for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store the tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Store eye drops at room temperature and keep the bottle tightly closed when not in use. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush medications down the toilet. Ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking moxifloxacin tablets within 4 to 8 hours of antacids containing magnesium or aluminum, sucralfate, multivitamins or supplements containing iron or zinc, or didanosine buffered tablets, as these can reduce the amount of medication your body absorbs. Avoid prolonged exposure to sunlight or tanning beds, as moxifloxacin can make your skin more sensitive to the sun — use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you, as it can cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Avoid strenuous physical activity, as moxifloxacin can rarely cause tendon damage. Avoid alcohol, as it may increase certain side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden pain, swelling, or tearing of a tendon (especially in the heel, shoulder, or hand); chest pain or irregular heartbeat or feel like your heart is pounding or fluttering; severe dizziness or fainting; muscle weakness or difficulty breathing; signs of a serious skin reaction such as blistering, peeling, or a widespread rash; severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody (which could happen even weeks after finishing the medication); signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing; new or worsening mental health symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations, anxiety, or thoughts of harming yourself; numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arms or legs; changes in vision or eye pain (if using eye drops). Also let your doctor know if your infection does not seem to be getting better after a few days.
when_it_works: Most people start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting moxifloxacin. However, it is very important that you finish the entire course of antibiotics your doctor prescribed, even if you feel completely better. Stopping too early can allow the bacteria to come back and may make the infection harder to treat.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): You may be at a higher risk of side effects such as tendon problems and heart rhythm changes. Talk to your doctor about your risks. Pregnant women: The safety of moxifloxacin during pregnancy has not been well established. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding mothers: It is not known if moxifloxacin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medication. Children: Moxifloxacin tablets are generally not recommended for children under 18 years of age. The eye drop form (Vigamox) may be used in children 4 months of age and older. Kidney or liver problems: The tablet form of moxifloxacin generally does not require a dose adjustment for kidney problems, but patients with severe liver disease should use it with caution. Always tell your doctor about all medical conditions you have.
